I am 68 years old, and I have worked these fields for 45 years. I only finished primary school, but the land has been my real teacher. My farm is 13.1 mu, and I grow wheat in winter and maize in summer — this is the double-cropping system every farmer around here in Quzhou County uses. My household has four people. My son and daughter-in-law work off-farm in the city, so my wife and I handle most of the farm work ourselves. Luckily, we have a well, so I am not completely at the mercy of the rain.

It is spring now. The winter wheat I sowed last October after ploughing the field is greening up. I will topdress nitrogen fertilizer soon and irrigate from my well at green-up, jointing, heading, and grain filling — four times in total if the spring stays dry. I will spray for weeds and insects two or three times. The seed is an improved variety from the county station, and if the weather cooperates, I expect around 500 kilograms per mu at harvest in early June.

Right after harvesting the wheat, I will plant hybrid maize on the same 13.1 mu. There is no time to waste — the summer season is short. I will run the rotary tiller over the stubble, apply base fertilizer, and then side-dress nitrogen when the maize is knee-high. I will irrigate two or three times from the well, especially at the jointing and filling stages, and spray pesticides two or three times for corn borers and weeds. With this management, I hope to get about 550 kilograms per mu from the maize.

This is what I have always done. It feeds my family, and the surplus grain brings in cash. I do not chase new fads — I stick to the practices I know work on my land.
